question: A 62-year-old man goes to the emergency room (ER) for an intense lower abdominal pain associated with inability to urinate. Physical examination shows tenderness of the lower abdomen bilaterally. Rectal examination reveals an enlarged, smooth, and symmetrical prostate. The ER team fails to pass a Foley catheter through the urethra, and the urology team decides to place a suprapubic catheter to drain the urine and relieve the patient’s symptoms. An ultrasound shows dilation of the collecting system in both kidneys. Laboratory studies show an elevated serum creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL for an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 50 ml/min/1.73 m2. The patient visits the urology team for a follow-up visit 3 weeks after the acute event, in which he claims to have close to normal urination. However, his serum creatinine stays elevated at 1.5 mg/dL. What renal gross findings correlate with this patient’s condition?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Enlarged prostate -> Urinary obstruction -> Increased pressure in urinary tract -> Dilation of collecting system in kidneys -> Possible renal parenchymal damage -> Elevated serum creatinine -> Possible chronic changes in kidney structure -> Enlarged kidneys with bosselated surface -> 85%

CHAIN: Urinary retention -> Back pressure on kidneys -> Dilation of renal pelvis and calyces -> Impaired renal function -> Elevated serum creatinine -> Possible chronic kidney changes -> Granular surface due to chronic damage -> 75%

CHAIN: Acute urinary obstruction -> Increased intrarenal pressure -> Compromised renal blood flow -> Renal parenchymal injury -> Persistent elevation of serum creatinine -> Possible compensatory changes in kidney structure -> Thin cortical rim due to atrophy -> 70%

CHAIN: Prostatic enlargement -> Urinary retention -> Hydronephrosis -> Renal function decline -> Elevated serum creatinine -> Chronic changes in kidney morphology -> Pale cortical deposits due to ischemia -> 60%
analysis: The patient's history of acute urinary retention due to an enlarged prostate leading to hydronephrosis and subsequent renal impairment suggests chronic kidney changes. The elevated serum creatinine despite improved urination indicates possible chronic kidney damage. The most likely renal gross finding in this scenario would be a granular surface, which is indicative of chronic kidney disease due to long-standing obstruction and damage.
